summary: This informational memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS accounting servers. It replaces RFC 2621 by deprecating the IPv4-only table and adding one supporting version-neutral IP addresses, and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to some objects.

plainLanguage.summary: This MIB gives network managers counters and status values for a RADIUS accounting server. It also adds a client table that can represent IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

questions: what is the radius accounting server mib
how does the mib represent ipv6 clients
subtitle: Management objects and counters for RADIUS accounting servers, including IP version-neutral client addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier RADIUS accounting server MIB used an IPv4-only address format for client entries.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4671 carries forward the server counters, deprecates the old client table, and adds an extended table with version-neutral address objects.
tldr.outcome: The memo obsoletes RFC 2621 and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to selected objects. It is Informational.

today: RFC 4671 is an Informational memo published in August 2006 that obsoletes RFC 2621. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Server MIB Measures
sections.content:
RFC 4671 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for a RADIUS accounting server. Management software generally accesses MIB objects through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

The module includes server-wide counters and a table with one row for each accounting client that shares a secret with the server. A device that acts as both a RADIUS client and server is expected to support both the client and server MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB exposes server status and counters to management software. It also records information about each accounting client known to the server.

sections.title: Replacing the IPv4-Only Client Table
sections.content:
RFC 4671 deprecates radiusAccClientTable, whose address object supports IPv4 only. It adds radiusAccClientExtTable with address-type and address objects for version-neutral IP addresses.

A server may keep the deprecated table for IPv4-only operation or compatibility with older management stations. If both tables contain a client, the corresponding row indexes should match, and the old table must not report an inaccurate address for a non-IPv4 client.
sections.plainLanguage: The new table can describe IPv4 and IPv6 clients. A server may keep the older table for compatibility, but it must not use it to report an address it cannot represent correctly.

sections.title: Counters and Reset Control
sections.content:
The module defines thirteen scalar objects and one client table. Its counters include requests, responses, duplicates, malformed requests, bad authenticators, dropped packets, requests not recorded, and unknown packet types.

The writable object radiusAccServConfigReset can reinitialize persistent server state when set to reset(2). When read, it reports another state such as initializing or running; it never returns the reset action value.
sections.plainLanguage: Managers can read totals for server activity and per-client counters. The reset object can restart persistent server state, so it needs controlled access.

sections.title: Keeping Older Management Support
sections.content:
The older table is marked deprecated, while the extended table is current. The RFC follows the recommendation to use one version-neutral address table rather than create separate tables for different IP versions.

An implementation may retain the old table when it only supports IPv4 or needs backward compatibility. It should create rows there only for addresses that the old format can represent accurately.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer table is the current one and supports multiple IP versions. The deprecated table can remain for older tools when its IPv4 addresses are accurate.

sections.title: Protecting Management Access
sections.content:
The reset object is read-write. Misuse can interrupt pending requests or cause a denial of service, depending on the implementation. Client address objects can also reveal information that could help someone attack a client.

The RFC recommends considering SNMPv3 authentication and privacy features and does not recommend earlier SNMP versions. Operators should control even read access to sensitive address objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Reset access can disrupt a server, and client addresses can be sensitive. The RFC recommends protecting management access and limiting who can read or change these objects.
